MST recognises the importance of transmission velocity as a media capability that affects the communication processes. Media with high levels of transmission velocity enable the sender and receiver to send and respond quickly, which improves coordination and focus (Dennis et al., 2008). As observed, face-to-face interaction with an AAC system and a non-disabled person consists of asymmetric transmission velocity. One party has low transmissio velocity because of the mediating role of the AAC system, and the other party has high transmission velocity as a person without the need for an AAC system for communication. Consistent with MST and our evaluation of context-aware user profiles, improving the transmission velocity for the AAC system user can support more coordi nation and shared understanding among the communication participants.

However, in this application of MST, there is an additional consideration. Proposition 1 of MST identifies that higher synchronicity media will improve communication performance for convergence communication pro cesses; lower synchronicity media will improve communication performance for conveyance communication processes. For many AAC system users, media synchronicity is extremely low primarily due to the AAC system' low levels of transmission velocity. Media synchronicity is “the extent to which the capabilities of a communication medium enable individuals to achieve synchronicity , and synchronicity is a state in which individuals are working together at the same time with a common focus” (Dennis et al., 2008, p. 581). Proposition 1 of MST likely assumes individuals are using communication media that do not have the same limitations as AAC systems for transmitting messages. Dennis et al. (2008) compare various types of communication media, such as face-to-face communication, email, instant messaging, fax and documents. While some AAC system user can receive and process information at the same rates of these communication media, other AAC system user with severe motor disabilities may experience transmission velocity more comparable to telegraph or sema phore. As a result, AAC system designers should improve transmission velocity in whatever means are possibl without concern for identifying if the communication task is comprised of mostly convergence or conveyance processes.

Design Principle 1. AAC system designers should improve transmission velocity for both conveyance and convergenc communication processes for AAC system users because of the low transmission rates in AAC systems for user with severe motor disabilities.

## 6.1.2 | Support alternative symbol sets

Context-aware user profiles provide a means to restrict the range of selection options available to an AAC system user. This filtering of options lessens the AAC system user's selection space, which provides a way to increase transmission velocity. Consistent with our observations of how context-aware user profiles could be used for meaningfu conversation, we suggest additional alternatives to improve symbol sets in AAC systems. For example, once th user's profile is established, the word basketball or a graphic of a basketball or favourite team logo could be th symbol used within the AAC system. This enables the user to select a single value as opposed to spelling out letter by letter the word, “basketball”, as a topic for conversation. Because the user profile is also context-aware, once “basketball” is selected, other choices could be presented based on user preferences, the time of year, team schedules and team performance. As another example of how we can vary or filter options for communication is the AAC system prototype developed specifically to enable individuals to communicate their medical and comfort needs more intuitively. The prototype (see Appendix A) enables AAC system users to select an area of the body, which narrow selection options to identify the area of the body that needs attention and the type of attention required

According to MST, another media capability that affects media synchronicity is the choice of symbol sets used for communication, including physical gestures, spoken word, written text, emojis and pictures. Proposition 4a and 4b state that more “natural symbol sets” and “a symbol set better suited to the content of the message” will support media synchronicity (Dennis et al., 2008, p. 586). With AAC systems, the symbols used, whether they are letters words, phrases, icons or other symbols that represent the intended message, affect the level of media synchronicit supported by the system.

In this research, we identified the critical role of symbol sets as a media capability that can improve the communication process for both medical and comfort needs (Design Requirement 2) and meaningful conversation (Design Requirement 3). With a context-aware user profile, the user can select among conversation topics based on the shared preferences and past interactions and the visitor. Some AAC systems already enable individuals to hav reduced symbol sets by enabling the user to choose among specific phrases for communication (McNaughton & Light, 2014). If these phrases are chosen based on generic or common phrases or words, then it may be difficult fo an AAC system user to share that they want to talk about last night's Toronto Raptors basketball game or that the want to face the window. Our AAC system prototype used body-focused symbols to enable AAC system users to easily select and communicate needs, such as being tired or wanting to face a different direction. The evaluation pro vides insights that alternative symbol sets can be used in conjunction with context-aware user profiles to furthe improve the communication process. Our research demonstrates that when the range of the communication topic is narrow (such as medical and comfort needs), symbol sets applicable to the intended message offers a means for AAC system users to express their needs (consistent with Proposition 4b in MST (Dennis et al., 2008)). However, additional creativity may be needed to extend similar creative symbol sets to improve media synchronicity when the con versation topic is wide-ranging or highly specific to the user (eg, meaningful conversation about hobbies, interests o family members).

Design Principle 2. AAC system designers should choose intuitive, specific, and narrow symbol sets for the AAC system user (as opposed to generic or non-specific symbol sets) to improve media synchronicity because of the low trans mission rates in AAC systems for users with severe motor disabilities

## 6.1.3 | Enable rehearsability

The fourth design requirement states that an AAC system user should be able to initiate communication with others Traditionally, many AAC system users can only respond to questions asked by the other parties in the conversation Our artificial evaluation (Section 4.3) and natural evaluation (Section 5) demonstrates the value of context-awar user profiles to enable an AAC system user to specify the topic of interest or identify the medical or comfort need without having to answer a series of questions by others. In addition to initiating topics of conversation or specifying a medical or comfort need without being asked, another opportunity to improve AAC system design is to enable users to queue messages for caregivers or other visitors during plentiful idle time. As explained in our discussion of the context of the problem, many individuals with severe motor disabilities spend large amounts of time alone. Fur thermore, many of these individuals we interacted with did not have access to an AAC system unless a researcher was present. Having an AAC system to develop messages for visitors before they arrive can facilitate the communi cation process and enable the AAC system user to initiate the communication process with a caregiver or loved one

According to MST, rehearsability reduces media synchronicity because it lowers the shared focus of the communica tion participants since the medium allows individuals to take more time in crafting messages (Dennis et al., 2008). Th delay in crafting and sending a message lowers the shared focus among the communication parties, meaning media syn chronicity is lower when the media capability of rehearsability is present. In this context, we propose that media synchro nicity can sometimes be improved or reduced by incorporating rehearsability, which is inconsistent with MST.

As context-aware user profiles and alternative symbol sets improve transmission velocity for AAC system users, a disparity between the transmission velocity for AAC system users and non-disabled users will still exist. The AAC system user must encode and transmit communication messages through an AAC system. Rehearsability that allows an AAC sys tem user to queue messages to expected visitors could improve media synchronicity to allow a conversation to occur as a visitor enters the room. The AAC system user would have the time to select and craft messages without the pressur of others watching and would have time to make corrections before the visitor's arrival. This would improve the commu nication process for the AAC user to enable them to initiate topics of conversations with visitors

Furthermore, the AAC system could support rehearsability by enabling the AAC system user to confirm that th selection was correct before displaying the result to the other conversational participant. If the user meant to select “Ears sore”, but accidentally selected “Head sore”, the caregiver would begin an unnecessary intervention that ma result in additional pain. Enabling the AAC user to confirm the message before sharing it with others would limit th number of errors and provide further improvement to the communication process.

However, rehearsability that allows the AAC system user to confirm a message before the other party receive the message would slow down transmission velocity, consistent with Proposition 5 of MST. If a message is not queued, the non-AAC system user must wait for the AAC system user to not only encode the message in the system through selection, but also confirm or correct the message. While rehearsability reduces transmission velocity rehearsability could improve shared understanding among conversational participants. Since the communication pro cess seeks to arrive at shared understanding (Dennis et al., 2008), rehearsability can still improve the communication process even if transmission velocity is slower with this design feature

Design Principle 3. AAC system designers should improve rehearsability for AAC system users to improve communicatio processes because rehearsability empowers the AAC system user to initiate communication with others.

## 6.1.4 | Encourage adaptability

Design requirement 5 states the need for a solution to allow an AAC system user to engage in communication across a range of conversational participants, both familiar and unfamiliar. Through our observations of individuals wit severe motor disabilities, many lived at a facility and some received care at home. Most of the time, these individual were around familiar people, such as loved ones or caregivers who regularly attended to their physical, medical, and comfort needs. However, sometimes new visitors, such as a new caregiver or a new friend or family member, woul want to engage in conversation with the individual. When an unfamiliar person engages in conversations, there can be challenges in reading communication cues with or without an AAC system. Our context-aware user profile design addresses this issue by creating a user profile for the AAC system user and familiar visitors. Known visitors woul have an established profile, and the system could adapt based on the past interactions between the user and visitor Unknown visitors would not have an established profile, and the AAC system could offer different choices to th AAC system user to adapt to this circumstance

MST acknowledges differences in communication processes as contexts and parties range from familiar to nove (Dennis et al., 2008). Proposition 7 of MST states that when tasks, media, and communication participants are more familiar, there is less need for media with high levels of media synchronicity; as tasks, media, and communication participants become less familiar, having media with higher levels of media synchronicity becomes more important. In this case, we are not advocating for decreasing the media's ability to support media synchronicity. However, we acknowledge that media synchronicity will likely be lower when elements of the context are unfamiliar. There is potential to improve the communication process by adapting AAC system elements, such as adjusting the symbo sets available for selection when an AAC system users engage with an unfamiliar visitor or topic. Additionally, the context-aware user profile could learn and adapt as topics and visitors become more familiar to the AAC sys tem user.

Design Principle 4. The AAC system should adapt to AAC system user needs by adapting elements (such as the context aware user profiles and symbol sets) to adjust for the familiarity of the conversational participants, tasks an media.

## 6.2 | Implications for theory and practice

We gained new insights related to MST through our DSR approach to improve communication processes for AAC users with severe motor disabilities. First, there can be a high degree of disparity in the transmission velocity among communication participants due to differences in the inputs used for the communication media, such as when a non disabled person and an AAC system user are engaging in a face-to-face conversation. In this scenario, the communi cation participants are face-to-face. One can communicate via speech, which ranges from 100 to 270 words pe minute (wpm); the other participant uses an AAC system with only 13 selections per minute. These individuals have different input rates for their communication media, which results in an unequal level transmission velocity among the conversation participants. This disparity in the rate of transmission velocity can occur in non-AAC system con texts as well. For example, assume two individuals are communicating via chat message. One communication partici pant uses a computer with keyboard as the input device and types at a speed of 80 wpm; the other participant use a virtual keyboard on a smartphone as an input device and can only type at a speed of 25 wpm. Although the com munication media is the same (ie, chat), the transmission velocity can vary among the individuals in part due to differences in the input devices used.

Little research has specifically examined transmission velocity in the context of MST (eg, Wang, Pauleen, & Zhang, 2016). Future research could more specifically examine the role of transmission velocity and its impact in th communication process, particularly if there are differences in the rate of input among individuals using a communi cation media. MST, as developed and described by Dennis et al. (2008), does not consider variations in transmission velocity among communication participants. Therefore, future research could examine whether transmission velocity disparities among communication participants is a potential boundary condition that affects the propositions identi fied within MST

Second, although MST defines tasks broadly, the communication media typically considered part of this theory has been more consistent with a workplace (eg, face-to-face, telephone, email, fax, documents, among others) and activities that occur in a work environment. However, the theory is broad enough to enable applications of MST to a range of contexts, such as education (Sun & Wang, 2017) or humanitarian efforts (Muhren et al., 2009). While ther are some stated boundary conditions of MST, such as the expectation that individuals are seeking to collaborat (as opposed to deceive) during communication, there may be other boundary conditions of this theory to explore, particularly as it relates to identifying the minimum levels of media capabilities required for synchronicity. If medi synchronicity is low due to low levels of specific media capabilities (eg, transmission velocity of the AAC system) then certain propositions regarding the need for lower levels of media synchronicity for certain types of communication processes may become irrelevant. Media capabilities can degrade in certain contexts, such as natural or manmade disasters, when communication media (eg, phone and internet service) are unavailable or exhibit latency at a time when communication is necessary. Our context reveals the need to examine the minimum threshold for media synchronicity before considering whether media synchronicity needs to be adjusted higher or lower to support con veyance or convergence processes. This provides an interesting opportunity for additional research to examine the minimal levels of media synchronicity needed to support various propositions within MST.

Also, several elements of MST extended quite well to our research context and offered additional insight on communication processes. Considering how various communication tasks with a person with severe motor disabil ities can have differing degrees of conveyance and convergence communication processes offers insights on how AAC systems need to adapt and shift to changing environments. One implication for both research and practice is for AAC system designers to consider the need for flexibility in AAC systems when creating these systems.

As a contribution to practice, we develop and explain how context-aware user profiles offer one potential solu tion to address the design requirements and design principles. Context-aware user profiles offer an opportunity to improve multiple media capabilities simultaneously, which increases media synchronicity. In addition, context-awar user profiles help humanise individuals with severe motor disabilities by highlighting their shared interests wit others.

We also identify a series of design principles, informed by the theoretical lens of MST, to identify how to improve media synchronicity for AAC system users. We specifically created these design principles to be indepen dent of the use of context-aware user profiles to achieve these goals. This approach yields flexibility for others that seek to find alternative options (as opposed to context-aware user profiles) to address the problem identified in thi research.

Developing AAC systems with increased media synchronicity provides an opportunity to increase the quality of life for an individual with severe motor disabilities. AAC systems using context-aware user profiles and embracing the design principles could enable the individual with a severe motor disability to better express their needs to care givers and maintain and establish social relationships with loved ones. Caregivers, such as doctors and nurses, could provide a better standard of care by knowing more about the needs and preferences of a patient who has little abilit to communicate with others, leading to a better patient–caregiver relationship. Friends and family could have mor engaging conversations and better understand the hopes, desires, and interests with an individual who must commu nicate using an AAC system.

This research can also stimulate new ideas on how to further improve AAC systems' design beyond the communication process itself. While our research intent and research approach focused on how to improve the communication process, the benefits of context-aware user profiles could provide additional benefits. For example, integrating an individual's electronic medical record with the context-aware user profile could improve one's medical care. An individual expressing specific combinations of medical needs or a frequent request for the medical or comfort need may indicate a problem that needs to be addressed (eg, warning sign for potential illness, adjustment needed to bed ding). The AAC system could also be a source of information, particularly to new caregivers or visitors about the individuals' preferences, current mood, and preferred conversation topics, which can generate rapport and improve the quality of interactions for both the individual with the severe motor disability and the visitor.<sup>4</sup>

## 6.3 | Limitations and future research

Our Strategy 2 approach (Iivari, 2015) and outcome-focused DSR methodology (Peffers et al., 2018) provided both opportunities and challenges. We began this research effort with a specific context in mind (ie, individuals with severe motor disabilities using AAC systems). We were able to identify a solution to address a specific need by creat ing a new design of AAC systems, one with context-aware user profiles. However, this approach to identifying research question and solution can present challenges in identifying opportunities to provide insights and generalisa tions beyond the initial context (Iivari, 2015). To achieve this goal, we provide a set of design principles related to AAC system design based on our research findings and the theoretical lens of MST.

Additional limitations of our research are related to our approach to evaluating our artefact. Implementing and embedding context-aware user profiles within an AAC system is quite complicated, particularly when working wit individuals with severe motor disabilities. For example, we could not incorporate a context-aware user profile to examine if this intervention would allow Todd to engage in meaningful conversations with others because Todd pas sed away during this research study. Hence, the evaluation remains at the conceptual level. Furthermore, there ar logistical challenges to identifying participants, obtaining consent among participants, and controlling for disabilit differences if we were to include the intended population of AAC system users within the study. Our protocol is consistent with other studies that evaluate assistive technologies on non-disabled participants first. Future researc should further develop implementations of context-aware user profiles and the design principles within AAC system and evaluate these systems among AAC system users with motor disabilities

Our artefact design and design principles found support to develop AAC systems with improvements in thre media capabilities identified in MST: transmission velocity, symbol sets, and rehearsability. We did not consider how parallelism or reprocessibility could be included or excluded to affect media synchronicity among AAC system users Future research should consider additional media capabilities that can further improve media synchronicity for AAC system users with severe motor disabilities.

Finally, the scope of our research has focused on individuals with severe motor disabilities that impact com munication. Our research considered individuals with full cognitive and sensory abilities (eg, sight and hearing) We did not consider the design of AAC systems for those with cognitive or other sensory disabilities. Further more, many individuals within this population with severe motor disabilities may have conditions that worsen over time. Individuals with diseases or disorders that cause progressively worse symptoms may experience a decline in their cognitive and sensory abilities. As a result, the individual, unfortunately, may no longer be able to use the original AAC system or the system would need to adapt to the individual's abilities. Future research ma consider developing systems or design principles to support individuals who have disabilities that become pro gressively worse over time.

## 7 | CONCLUSION

This research seeks to identify how to improve the design of AAC systems to improve communication processes for individuals with severe motor disabilities. To achieve this goal, we used a DSR process to identify a possible solution: context-aware user profiles incorporated in the design of AAC systems. We evaluated how context-aware user pro files could support AAC system users with severe motor disabilities to engage in conversations about medical and comfort needs and more meaningful conversations with visitors. We examined our findings using the theoretical lens of MST to identify design principles that can be used by AAC system designers to improve communication processes for AAC system users. While our design principles are consistent with the incorporation of context-aware user profiles within an AAC system, this prescriptive knowledge is abstract enough to encourage others to consider addi tional solutions to further improve the design of AAC systems. We also identified implications for theory an practice based on our findings. Our results are intended to improve communication processes that would enabl individuals with severe motor disabilities to experience significant enhancements in their quality of life, thereb enabling them to participate in society more fully.

## AUTHOR BIOGRAPHIES

Adriane B. Randolph is the Founder and Executive Director of the BrainLab and Professor of Information Systems in the Michael J. Coles College of Business at Kennesaw State University. She designs brain–computer interface systems, which allow hands-free control of technology for people living locked-in to their bodies and reflect varying cognitive states. Her research spans human-computer interaction, neuro-information systems and neuro-education. She serves as a longtime program co-chair for the international NeuroIS Retreat and is a founding member of the NeuroIS Society and the BCI Society. Her related work has appeared in the International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction, AIS Transactions on Human Computer Interaction, Communica tions of the AIS and the ACM Transactions on Accessible Computing

Stacie C. Petter is the Ben H. Williams Professor of Information Systems & Business Analytics at Baylor University's Hankamer School of Business. Her current research examines the impacts of information systems (including an emphasis on responsible research), research methodology, and online gaming and gamification. Her work appears in outlets including MIS Quarterly, Journal of Management Information Systems, European Journal of Information Systems, Journal of the Association for Information Systems, among others. She previously served as editor-in-chief of The DATABASE for Advances in Information Systems, associate editor for MIS Quarterly and Information Systems Journal, and she is currently a senior editor for AIS Transactions on Replication Research and a member of the editorial review board for the Journal of the Association for Information Systems

Veda C. Storey is the Tull Professor of Computer Information Systems and professor of computer science at the J. Mack Robinson College of Business, Georgia State University. Her research interests are in intelligent information systems, data management, conceptual modelling and design science research. She is particularly interested in the assessment of the impact of new technologies on business and society from a data management perspective. Dr. Storey is a member of the steering committee of the International Conference of Conceptua Modeling and a recipient of the Peter P. Chen Award.

Melody M. Jackson is the Director of the Georgia Tech BrainLab, whose mission is to research innovative human-computer interaction for people with severe disabilities, including direct brain interfaces and other biometric interfaces. She and her team have researched ways of improving communication, environmental control, mobility and stroke rehabilitation with brain signal control. The BrainLab's current work also includes mobile Brain–Computer Interfaces for mainstream users. Her work has been funded by the National Science Foundation, National Institutes of Health (NINDS), NIDRR and DARPA.

## A. APPENDIX: DEVELOPMENT OF A MEDICAL COMFORT ONTOLOGY

Before we could create a context-aware AAC system for medical and comfort needs, we needed an ontology for thi domain. To create a medical comfort ontology, we extracted information regarding the comfort and care of peopl with severe motor disabilities, terms and phrases from various sources, including related literature and patient observation. One source of content to develop the ontology is an article entitled The Locked-In Syndrome (translate from French) by Philippe Van Eeckhout (1997) that provides many details pertaining to the medical conditions of those suffering from severe motor disabilities. For example, Van Eeckhout describes troubles with eye movement and the paralysis of side-to-side movement of the eyes. From this information, the phrase, “I can't see”, and others, is inferred using a high-level form of natural language processing; here, a researcher used real-world knowledge to make inferences rather than rely on a computer system to make interpretations. We also analysed transcripts and notes based on interactions with individuals with severe motor disabilities. Table A1 identifies these sources of data

After extracting information from multiple sources, terms and phrases were organised into a medical comfort domain ontology for individuals with severe motor disabilities as shown in Table A2. A domain ontology captures th

To incorporate the medical comfort ontology as part of the AAC system, we considered how we might design a new AAC system to enable AAC system users to identify their medical and comfort needs more easily. We used a scanning interface where the selection mechanism proceeded at pre-set intervals of 3 seconds. The “body parts”

![](/api/attachments/EP93WR89/fulltext/images/0dc3b4d6430c28785fa03b646cc25dc6eb14c5bbc5e7a9fc0aaa43f330d6caef.jpg)  
F I G U R E A 2 AAC system without context-aware user profile [Colour figure can be viewed at wileyonlinelibrary.com]

section of the domain was represented graphically with an abstract picture of a human form in three sections: head trunk and legs. The space bar on a standard keyboard was used for selection input to emulate the “yes/no” response capabilities of an AAC system user with severe motor disabilities. When a section of the body was selected, addi tional body parts were presented on the screen for the next level of selection. As selections were made, the user had different options to choose from related to the body part. Figure A1 shows screen shots of the prototype (based on the medical comfort ontology) for the AAC system user to transmit the message “Ears sore”.

Figure A2 provides screen shots of the AAC system with the context-aware user profile for transmitting the message “Ears sore”. There are fewer selection options for the individual since the symbol set is based on the information provided in the user profile

With or without the use of context-aware user profiles, this type of AAC system enables a user to express their medical or comfort needs to others more easily through an easy-to-use interface created specifically for this purpose AAC system users make fewer selections with this type of system, which is one way to increase the rate of communication.

# Assessing and Enhancing Adversarial Robustness of Predictive Analytics: An Empirically Tested Design Framework

Weifeng Li<sup>a</sup> and Yidong Chai<sup>b</sup>

<sup>a</sup>Department of Management Information Systems, Terry College of Business, University of Georgia, Athens GA, USA; <sup>b</sup>School of Management, Hefei University of Technology, Key Laboratory of Process Optimization and Intelligence Decision Making, Ministry of Education, Hefei University of Technology, Hefei, China

## ABSTRACT

As predictive analytics increasingly applies supervised machine learning (SML) models to inform mission-critical decision-making, adversaries become incentivized to exploit the vulnerabilities of these SML models and mislead predictive analytics into erroneous decisions. Due to the limited understanding and awareness of such adversarial attacks, the predictive analytics knowledge and deployment need a principled technique for adversarial robustness assessment and enhancement. In this research, we leverage the technology threat avoidance theory as the kernel theory and propose a research framework for assessing and enhancing the adversarial robustness of predictive analytics applications. We instantiate the proposed framework by developing a robust text classification system, the ARText system. The proposed system is rigorously evaluated in comparison with benchmark methods on two tasks extensively enabled by SML: spam review detection and spam email detection, which then confirmed the utility and efectiveness of our ARText system. Results from numerous experiments revealed that our proposed framework could significantly enhance the adversarial robustness of predictive analytics applications.

## KEYWORDS

Predictive analytics; adversarial robustness; text mining; artificial intelligence security; supervised machine learning; design frameworks

## Introduction

The recent advancement in machine learning and the increasing availability of big data have encouraged organizations to apply predictive analytics to inform mission-critical decisionmaking [14, 25, 32, 48]. Such predictive analytics applications often leverage a supervised machine learning (SML) model to make empirical predictions based on the patterns captured from the data [48]. For example, review platforms leverage text classification to detect spam reviews [33]; email service providers leverage classification models to filter out spam emails [17]; mobile app platforms utilize text mining and image processing to detect fraudulent apps based on app descriptions and icons [57]; financial institutions predict default rate by leveraging borrower information [8]; human resources use SML to assist job candidate selection [60]; healthcare practitioner discover treatment barriers from patient communities [58]; and autonomous vehicles leverage sensory data to predict energy eficiency [50].

Despite its enormous potential, predictive analytics is not without its pitfalls. One emerging threat to predictive analytics has proven to be particularly problematic: adversarial attacks [23]. As SML-enabled predictive analytics become an integral part of organizational decision-making, adversaries are incentivized to exploit the vulnerabilities of SML models underlying predictive analytics applications and mislead these applications into making erroneous decisions favoring the adversaries. In particular, such adversarial attacks often involve meticulously perturbing the input to the target SML model for achieving the desired output. This could be concerning for predictive analytics applied in the domains where the input is provided by the individual who is immediately afected by the decision made by the SML model [8, 13, 60]. Examples of such application domains include spam detection [33], fraud detection [1], credit approval [8, 59], employee hiring [8, 59], and student admission [8, 59]. In particular, a spam review could be meticulously modified to bypass the spam review detection system and spam emails could be deliberately designed to deceive SML-based spam email filtering systems. Such adversarial attacks on SML models could undermine the decision-making enabled by predictive analytics, leading to potential reputation damages and financial losses.

The vulnerability of SML models is not new and has received increasing attention from the research communities [8, 13, 18, 23, 26]. Nonetheless, it warrants further investigation in the emerging applications of predictive analytics for three reasons. First, organizations have increasingly applied SML-enabled predictive analytics into their mission-critical business processes [11, 20]; however, predictive analytics in information system (IS) research has not fully acknowledged the potential security threat against the vulnerabilities of the underlying SML models. There is limited understanding and awareness of the issue in the predictive analytics literature to provide guidelines for organizations utilizing predictive analytics taking inputs from potentially unreliable sources. Second, the IS literature focuses the evaluation of predictive analytics primarily on the models’ predictive performance, such as accuracy [34, 48]. The systematic assessment of predictive analytics applications’ robustness to adversarial exploitation has been generally understudied. As organizations decision-making about predictive analytics is informed by its evaluation, there is a need for adversarial robustness assessment techniques to complement the existing practice of evaluating predictive analytics applications. Third, the limited awareness of adversarial attacks and the lack of robustness assessment have resulted in the deployment of predictive analytics applications that are potentially vulnerable to adversarial attacks. The exploitation of such applications could lead to financial losses, reputation damages, and health and safety risks, impeding the realization of predictive analytics’ enormous potential. As such, there is an urgent need for enhancing the adversarial robustness of these deployed predictive analytics applications to adversarial exploitation.

In this paper, we seek to address two critical research questions relating to the adversarial robustness of predictive analytics applications: (1) How to assess the robustness of predictive analytics applications to adversarial attacks? (2) How to improve the robustness of predictive analytics applications in an adversarial context? Drawing upon the technology threat avoidance theory, we propose a research framework for assessing and enhancing the adversarial robustness of predictive analytics applications. The research framework seeks to provide a principled approach for improving the adversarial robustness of existing predictive analytics applications. We further instantiate the proposed framework by developing a robust text classification system. Leveraging the technology threat avoidance theory as a kernel theory, our proposed framework comprises a novel assessment model for evaluating the adversarial robustness of a predictive analytics application, and design principles for enhancing the adversarial robustness of predictive analytics applications. We demonstrate the efectiveness of our framework in the context of text classification tasks. In particular, we develop the ARText system, which jointly incorporates ensemble learning and adversarial retraining to improve its robustness to adversarial attacks. To rigorously evaluate our proposed system, we conducted two sets of evaluations on the testbeds of spam review detection and spam email detection. The first set of evaluations examined the utility of our proposed adversarial robustness assessment. The second set of evaluations gauged the eficacy of our proposed system in enhancing adversarial robustness. Overall, the ARText system was able to outperform baseline models in detecting adversarial spam reviews, indicating the efectiveness of our proposed design framework.

## Research Background

## Predictive Analytics in IS

Predictive analytics leveraging SML models are becoming prevalent in various business contexts, including spam detection [3, 33], fraud detection [54, 57], credit approval [8, 59], student admission [8, 59], marketing [19, 22], and crowdsourcing [56]. Most predictive analytics applications draw upon the statistical learning theory to utilize or develop SML models. The statistical learning theory formalizes the predictive task as choosing a model $f : X \to Y ;$ , where X is the input space and Y is the output space, such that for a given input $x \in X , f$ predicts the corresponding output $y \in Y$ [53]. For example, detecting review manipulation could be formulated as identifying a model that predicts the spam review label given the review text and reviewer attributes [33]. The optimal model is chosen by applying the empirical risk minimization (ERM) principle on a training set containing l samples of input-output pairs. Specifically, the ERM principle finds the function that minimizes the loss $\mathcal { L } ( f ( x ) , y )$ between the output y to a given input x and the prediction f ðxÞ made by the function on the training set: $\operatorname* { m i n } _ { f } { \frac { 1 } { l } } \sum _ { i = i } ^ { l } { \mathcal { L } } ( f ( x _ { i } ) , y _ { i } )$ . The loss function could be the squared error $\left( y _ { i } - f ( x _ { i } ) \right) ^ { 2 }$ for regression tasks where $\gamma \mathrm { { s } }$ are continuous outputs, and the misclassification indicator function $1 ( y _ { i } = f ( x _ { i } ) )$ for classification tasks, where $\gamma \mathbf { \bar { s } }$ are discrete outputs.

The key assumption underlying the ERM principle is that all inputs x, including training inputs and unseen inputs from the actual application setting, are drawn independently from the same fixed distribution $P ( x )$ . Nonetheless, this assumption could be challenged in certain real-world application domains where the input that predictive analytics relies on to make a decision is provided by the individual who is immediately afected by the decision [13]. In such application domains, adversaries can meticulously manipulate the input data to trick SML models into favorable decisions and subsequently benefit from them [8, 60].

Examples of such application domains include including spam detection [33], credit approval [8, 59], employee hiring [8, 59], and student admission [8, 59]. Specifically, review spammers could meticulously write spam review content to bypass SML-based spam review detection systems. Similarly, spam emails could be deliberately designed to deceive SMLbased spam email filtering systems. Credit card applicants might provide fraudulent information to get approval from automated credit application processing systems. Job candidates might fake their background attributes in job applications to deceive human resources automation, and student candidates might alter their information to get admitted by automated student admission management systems. While these systems attempt to mitigate the adversarial exploitation by employing fraud detection systems, recent systems have extensively leveraged SML [1, 3, 33, 54, 57] and are, therefore, vulnerable to adversarial exploitation as well. Such threats against the SML model underlying predictive analytics necessitate the consideration of adversarial robustness when applying SML models.

However, the existing evaluation of predictive analytics primarily focuses on predictive performance, that is, the model’s ability to predict new observations accurately on testing datasets resembling the training datasets [48]. Such an evaluation procedure is insuficient for assessing the adversarial robustness of SML models in real-world application domains, where inputs can be perturbed to mislead SML models. For example, predictive analytics for classification tasks, such as detecting spam reviews and phishing websites, primarily use accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure (F1), and area under the receiver operating curve (ROC AUC) [3, 33]; predictive analytics for regression tasks, such as predicting sales, widely adopt mean absolute percentage error and root mean square of errors [22]; and predictive analytics for ranking tasks, such as recommender systems, often utilize top-k precision and rank correlation coeficient [19, 38]. These metrics cannot directly measure adversarial robustness. Hence, it is imperative to enrich the predictive analytics literature by developing a systematic adversarial robustness assessment model.

## Adversarial Attacks against SML Models

There are generally two attacking strategies against SML models: causative attacks and exploratory attacks [29]. Causative attacks, also known as poisoning attacks, manipulate the training data $\{ ( x _ { i } , y _ { i } ) | i \in [ 1 , \ldots , l ] \}$ to subvert the SML model. Exploratory attacks, also known as evasion attacks, mislead the trained SML model $f ( x )$ with meticulously designed inputs, known as adversarial samples. The adversarial sample is achieved by introducing a carefully designed perturbation $\delta$ to an original data point $x _ { i }$ in order to mislead a trained SML model to make erroneous decisions $( \boldsymbol { \mathrm { e . g . } } , f ( x _ { i } + \delta ) \not = f ( x _ { i } ) )$ while maintaining its main properties (e.g., the negativity of review content). For example, a fake negative review on the competitor might be easily intercepted by the spam review detection system of an online review platform. To bypass the detection system, the adversary can carefully perturb this review (e.g., replacing words, introducing typos) to exploit the vulnerability of the underlying SML model. For most predictive analytics applications, it is dificult for adversaries to have access to the training process of the target SML model and therefore exploratory attacks are potentially more prevalent than causative attacks. Table 1 provides a taxonomy of the state-of-the-art exploratory attacks.

Table 1. A taxonomy of the state-of-the-art exploratory attacks.

<table><tr><td>Knowledge Level</td><td>Attack Type</td><td>Example Attacks</td></tr><tr><td rowspan="2">White-Box</td><td>Maximal Loss</td><td>Fast Gradient Sign Method [24]</td></tr><tr><td>Minimal Perturbation</td><td>L-BFGS [12, 49], Jacobian-based Saliency Map Attack [47], Deepfool [41]</td></tr><tr><td rowspan="2">Black-Box</td><td>Transferability-based</td><td>Reservoir Sampling [46], Ensemble-based Approach [40]</td></tr><tr><td>Query-based</td><td>Feature Cross-substitution [35], Jacobian-based Dataset Augmentation [47], Gradient Estimation [6]</td></tr></table>

Note: L-BFGS, Limited Memory-Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno algorithm.

Tactics of exploratory attacks are primarily diferentiated based on adversaries’ knowledge about the target SML model f ðxÞ in terms of its structure, parameters, gradients, and other specifications. In white-box exploratory attacks, adversaries have the full knowledge about the target SML model f ðxÞ and leverage the knowledge to generate adversarial samples through constrained optimization. The two prominent types of white-box exploratory attacks are maximal loss attacks and minimal perturbation attacks. The objective of maximal loss attacks is to maximize the error made by the target SML model subject to the maximum allowable perturbation ε from the original sample (e.g., $\operatorname* { m a x } _ { \delta } \lvert f ( x _ { i } + \delta ) - f ( x _ { i } ) \rvert , \mathrm { s . t . ~ } \lvert \delta \rvert < \varepsilon )$ . As adversarial samples are allowed to perturb further from their original samples, adversaries have increased flexibility to generate adversarial samples, raising the efectiveness of these adversarial samples in misleading SML models and diminishing the target SML model’s predictive performance. However, excessive perturbation could entail a higher faking cost [13], and therefore the maximum allowable perturbation is imposed to reflect this constraint. The objective of minimal perturbation attacks is to trick the target SML model into making a certain erroneous decision (e.g., $f ( x _ { i } + \delta ) = t$ where t is the desired label diferent from $f ( x _ { i } ) )$ while minimizing the perturbation δ from the original data point (e.g., min δ; s:t: $f ( x _ { i } + \delta ) = t )$ . Whereas maximal loss attacks can generate adversarial samples much faster than minimal perturbation attacks [24], the minimal perturbation attack outperforms by generating adversarial samples with a higher success rate and a lower detection rate.

Black-box exploratory attacks are more prevalent for predictive analytics applications in practice, where adversaries have limited or no knowledge about the specification of target SML models. As such, the black-box exploratory attack aims to first recover the missing knowledge about the target SML model through approximation and then leverages the white-box attack tactic with the approximated information. In particular, there are two common types of black-box exploratory attacks: transferability-based attacks and querybased attacks.

The transferability of adversarial attacks refers to the finding that certain adversarial samples designed to mislead one SML model can also cause another SML model to make erroneous decisions, despite their distinctive model specifications [46]. In particular, both intra-model transferability and cross-model transferability exist among the SML models. The former is the transferability among SML models trained with the same model structure (e.g., decision tree) but diferent parameter initialization and training set, whereas the latter is the transferability among SML models with diferent model structures (e.g., a decision tree and a neural network). Transferability-based attacks seek to approximate the target SML model with a substitute SML model, which is expected to share common vulnerabilities with the target SML model [39]. Subsequently, an adversary could generate adversarial samples against the substitute model and use the generated adversarial samples to attack the target SML model [40]. The intra-model transferability attack requires the adversary to know the specific SML structure of the target model, and such information could be acquired through reconnaissance. For example, many fraud detection systems are documented in academic literature and patent documents, and some are open-sourced on Github. Adversaries could investigate these resources, key persons involved, and their employment history to infer the specific SML structure of a certain organization’s system. In contrast, the cross-model transferability attack does not require any information about the target model [40]. While the cross-model transferability attack might not be as efective as the intra-model transferability attack, the former has wider applicability and could be particularly useful where the target predictive analytics application does not limit the number of inputs it takes.

Query-based attacks primarily seek to reverse engineer the target SML model behavior through sending queries and collecting the target model outputs. Subsequently, adversaries can train a substitute SML model, such as Decision Tree, Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, and Deep Neural Networks, with data queried from the target SML model to imitate its model behavior [43]. Adversarial samples generated against this substitute model can be efective on the target SML model [6]. Existing query algorithms generally need a number of queries (e.g., proportional to the number of features) to be efective. In query-based attacks, the adversary needs to have the ability to repetitively query the target SML model with inputs and gather the corresponding model outputs. Such repetitive query access is quite common in several use-cases, such as spam review detection systems, spam email detection systems, and credit application processing systems. For example, adversaries could maintain multiple accounts on the review platform for submitting spam reviews and gather outputs based on whether the spam reviews are taken down by the target system. Moreover, in certain domains, historical data of model inputs and outputs could be collected from the target SML model, which could also train the substitute model for query-based attacks. For instance, Yelp publishes a dataset of spam and genuine reviews as determined by its renowned spam review filter for academic research purposes, which could be leveraged for training a substitute model [42].

## Defense against Adversarial Attacks

The IS literature has examined the defense of exploratory adversarial attacks from the perspective of the principal-agent model, where the principal leverages an SML model (e.g., a classifier) to make a decision (e.g., fraud, admission, credit approval) based on the data provided by the agent [7]. The adversarial agent has the incentive to strategically perturb the data provided to the principal in order to attain a favorable decision. In anticipation of the possible strategic perturbation, the principal can defend the SML model by incorporating the perturbation into the model optimization. Specifically, an enhanced support vector machine (SVM) capable of prohibiting adversaries constrained by a certain perturbation range has been developed by solving a Nash equilibrium between the principal and the adversarial agent through mixed integer programming [8]. Since numerically solving the mixed integer program can be computationally intensive, the genetic algorithm has been utilized to expedite the process by approximating the solution [10]. The genetic algorithm is further extended to address adversarial attacks where the inputs are composed of only binary variables [9]. Relatedly, the particular perturbation type of hiding data has been studied and the defensive measure of data imputation methods has been proposed for SVM [59] and support vector regression [60].

We seek to complement the existing IS literature on defense against adversarial attacks in several ways. First, while prior research extensively studies SVM and develops defensive measures with analytical solutions specific to this type of SML model, it is unclear whether defending other types of SML models (e.g., models with non-linear discriminant functions) can be solved with analytical solutions. Many predictive analytics applications leverage SML models other than SVM as their underlying SML models, and therefore we aim to develop a generalized approach for enhancing the SML models in these predictive analytics applications.

Second, past literature mostly studies the white-box exploratory attack which assumes the adversaries to have the full knowledge of the target SML model. We extend the literature by investigating the black-box exploratory attack where limited knowledge of the target SML model other than its outputs is available to adversaries. The black-box exploratory attack is common to numerous domains, such as fraud detection, spam detection, credit approval, employee hiring, and student admission. Adversaries targeting these domains often have little knowledge about the SML models but can repetitively access the model outputs given inputs.

Third, existing research based on the principal-agent model assumes all individuals interacting with predictive analytics applications are rational and have incentives to perturb the input data for favorable output. Our research allows for benign agents who truthfully report the input data. This is reasonable in several use-cases such as online review platforms, credit card applications, employee hiring, and student admission, where not all individuals intend to commit fraud.

In summary, this research seeks to address the black-box adversarial attack, where the predictive analytics application makes decisions about individuals based on the input provided by them, and adversaries aim to mislead the predictive analytics application into favorable decisions. In particular, the predictive analytics application makes decisions by minimizing the loss caused by incorrect decisions in anticipation of adversarial perturbation in inputs and the adversary has repetitive access to predictive analytics outputs but limited information about the underlying SML model specifications.

## Framework for Adversarial Robustness Assessment and Enhancement

Efective countermeasures against the black-box exploratory attacks to SML models entail the utilization of an IS security theory to provide design guidelines. Grounded in cybernetics theory and coping theory, technology threat avoidance theory (TTAT) serves as an appropriate kernel theory governing the design requirements of our proposed framework. TTAT expounds on the process for mitigating and addressing information technology (IT)

![](/api/attachments/PXHJ4MQQ/fulltext/images/820203ed581fb0c6e8de9890bd789d1a2a8a4a3254e5f297d61156adf5b09403.jpg)  
Figure 1. The framework for assessing and enhancing adversarial robustness of predictive analytics.

threats, which consists of two major components: threat appraisal and threat coping [39]. In threat appraisal, the susceptibility of the system and the negative consequences of the IT threat is evaluated [44]. In threat coping, safeguarding measures are taken to avoid the IT threat. Mitigating and addressing black-box exploratory attacks requires the inclusion of both components: threat appraisal and threat coping. Therefore, efective defensive measures against adversarial attacks entail consideration of a framework capable of appraising the threat to the SML model imposed by adversarial attacks and coping with the threat to safeguard the SML model. As such, our proposed design framework, as shown in Figure 1, consists of two major meta-requirements [55]: adversarial robustness assessment (corresponding to threat appraisal) and adversarial robustness enhancement (corresponding to threat coping). The adversarial robustness assessment meta-requirement primarily seeks to appraise the susceptibility of the SML model to adversarial attacks. The adversarial robustness enhancement meta-requirement mainly aims to cope with adversarial attacks through strengthening the resilience of the SML model to adversarial attacks. Specifically, the framework enhances its ability to cope with adversarial attacks through ensemble learning and adversarial retraining. The subsequent sections elaborate on the meta-design for each meta-requirement.

## Adversarial Robustness Assessment

Drawing upon the existing practices, we propose to quantify the adversarial robustness of the SML model through empirical analysis. In particular, the empirical adversarial robustness measures a model’s robustness to a set of adversarial samples through the impact of adversarial samples on the model’s predictive performance. In particular, our proposed adversarial robustness assessment involves two steps: (1) adversarial sample generation and (2) adversarial robustness measurement. The former aims to emulate adversarial attacks by generating adversarial samples, whereas the latter seeks to measure the model’s adversarial robustness on testbeds containing emulated adversarial attacks. The first step generates adversarial samples with a domain-relevant and state-of-the-art adversarial sample generation algorithm. Most adversarial example generation algorithms are domain-specific: an adversarial sample generation algorithm designed for images might not be as efective in generating adversarial textual samples. Moreover, as weak adversarial samples that are easy to defend could lead to overestimating the adversarial robustness, strong adversarial samples generated by the state-of-the-art benchmark adversarial sample algorithm can reflect the model’s adversarial robustness in real-world applications more accurately.

Table 2. Various adversarial robustness definition and quantification.

<table><tr><td>Category</td><td>Description</td><td>Examples</td></tr><tr><td>Performance-based Measure</td><td>Effectiveness of an SML model in fulfilling a task on adversarial samples</td><td>Robustness accuracy [23], Genetic attack accuracy [30], Evasion robustness [51]</td></tr><tr><td>Perturbation-based Measure</td><td>Cost of modifying an original sample into a successful adversarial sample</td><td> $L_0$ ,  $L_2$ , and  $L_\infty$  norms [12], adversarial frequency and severity [5]</td></tr></table>

Note: SML, supervised machine learning.

A summary of the existing practice of adversarial robustness measurement is provided in Table 2. Adversarial robustness definition and quantification can be classified into two broad categories: performance-based adversarial robustness and perturbation-based adversarial robustness.

The performance-based adversarial robustness gauges the SML model’s predictive performance, under adversarial attacks of a given set of adversarial samples, in fulfilling a task (e.g., text classification, image classification). A relatively high predictive performance of the SML model on adversarial samples suggests that the SML model possesses high robustness to adversarial attacks. One common performance-based adversarial robustness measure is robustness accuracy, which measures the accuracy of the classification model on adversarial samples. Despite their usefulness, the existing measures of performance-based adversarial robustness are mostly based on the absolute predictive performance under adversarial attacks, which could raise validity concerns due to convoluting the measurement of adversarial robustness with that of predictive performance. Moreover, the robustness assessment testbed comprises only adversarial samples, which might overrepresent the adversarial attacks in real-world application domains.

While the performance-based adversarial robustness measures are conditioned on the perturbation range pre-specified by the maximum allowable perturbation, adversaries in real-world attacks might not be always bounded by the specified perturbation range in the robustness assessment. As the perturbation range expands, the SML model could become less robust to adversarial attacks. To that end, the perturbation-based adversarial robustness takes into consideration the cost of perturbing an original sample into a successful adversarial sample. The cost is quantified by the deviation between the successful adversarial sample and its corresponding original sample in $L _ { p }$ norms [12].<sup>1</sup> One common perturbation-based adversarial robustness measure is $L _ { 2 }$ norm, which gauges the Euclidean distance between the successful adversarial sample and its original sample. The overall adversarial robustness of the SML model is reported using certain descriptive statistics of the $L _ { p }$ norm similarity distances for each pair of samples, such as the minimum and the average. Nonetheless, the simple descriptive statistics might not fully capture the trade-of between the perturbation range of adversarial attacks and their impact on the SML model’s predictive performance, which could be critical to decision-making in the design and deployment of predictive analytics.

As such, we propose the meta-design of two adversarial robustness measures to complement existing predictive performance measures in evaluating organizational predictive analytics applications. Specifically, we propose that performance-based robustness measures should concentrate on evaluating SML models’ adversarial robustness by teasing out the predictive performance from the adversarial robustness using relative measures. Moreover, testbeds for robustness assessment should reflect realistic settings by including both adversarial and non-adversarial samples. We further propose that perturbation-based robustness measures should capture the trade-of between the perturbation range of adversarial attacks and their impact on predictive performance. Such trade-of enables a comprehensive understanding of the robustness of SML models in applications where adversaries are not bounded by a fixed perturbation range.

## Adversarial Robustness Enhancement

Existing research on defending black-box exploratory attacks mainly focuses on developing attack-specific defensive measures [30, 31, 51]. While efective, these attack-specific defensive measures might not be suitable for the real-world application domains, where the specific types of adversarial attacks are often unknown. To efectively improve the adversarial robustness of SML models, our meta-design proposes to mitigate black-box exploratory attacks with two design principles: ensemble learning and adversarial retraining. The former informs the architecture of a robust SML model, and the latter provides the guideline for training the SML model process for adversarial robustness.

Ensemble learning is the practice of harnessing the collective power of multiple SML models on the same task to enhance predictive performance, which has the potential to improve adversarial robustness. On the one hand, ensemble learning efectively mitigates the security risk of exploitation with diversification [15]. With the traditional practice of using one single SML model, the shared vulnerabilities between this SML model and the adversary’s substitute model lead to correlated failure, forming the basis of transferabilitybased attacks [46]. To that end, ensemble learning leverages the diversification strategy such that an adversarial sample needs to mislead the majority of the SML models in the ensemble for the attack to be successful. Generating an adversarial sample capable of simultaneously misleading multiple SML models is perceivably more dificult than generating an adversarial sample capable of deceiving one single SML model. On the other hand, ensemble learning increases the dificulty for adversaries to develop efective substitute models. Combining multiple SML models together, the ensemble learning model exponentially expands the function space in which adversaries need to search for their substitute models. In comparison with approximating one single SML model, developing substitute models for ensemble learning requires identifying the right combination of constituent models, approximating each constituent model, and using the correct type of ensembles (e.g., Bootstrap aggregating, boosting, stacking), none of which is trivial to adversaries.

Adversarial retraining involves training the target SML model with the original training set augmented with adversarial samples [36]. Adversarial retraining improves adversarial robustness because incorporating adversarial samples into the training set is mathematically equivalent to explicitly modeling adversarial risk in the SML model’s objective function. We illustrate this by examining the objective function after incorporating adversarial samples. Suppose the training set is $( x , y )$ , where x is the inputs and y is the corresponding outputs. Without loss of generality, we assume the target SML model $f _ { \beta } ( x _ { i } )$ minimizes the objective loss function in the form of $\begin{array} { r } { \underset { \beta } { \operatorname* { m i n } } \frac { 1 } { \left| x \right| } \sum _ { x _ { i } \in x , y _ { i } \in y } \mathcal { L } \left( f _ { \beta } ( x _ { i } ) , y _ { i } \right) } \end{array}$ , where $\beta$ is the model’s parameter vector and $\mathcal { L } ( \cdot )$ is the task-specific loss function. Suppose we have an adversarial dataset $( x ^ { \mathrm { A } } , y ^ { \mathrm { A } } )$ , where $x ^ { \mathrm { A } }$ are adversarial inputs and $y ^ { \mathrm { A } }$ is the correct outputs of the corresponding original data points. Drawing upon the empirical risk management principle, incorporating these adversarial samples into the loss function results in a loss function with two terms:

$$
\min _ {\beta} \frac {1}{| x | + | x ^ {\mathrm{A}} |} \left(\Sigma_ {x _ {i} \in x, y _ {i} \in y} \mathcal {L} \big (f _ {\beta} (x _ {i}), y _ {i} \big) + \Sigma_ {x _ {j} \in x ^ {\mathrm{A}}, y _ {j} \in y ^ {\mathrm{A}}} \mathcal {L} \big (f _ {\beta} (x _ {j}), y _ {j} \big)\right),
$$

where the first term in the parenthesis is the loss caused by the original training set, and the second term is the loss caused by adversarial samples, which captures the adversarial risk. While minimizing the first term enhances the SML model’s predictive performance, minimizing the second term improves the SML model’s adversarial robustness. Moreover, in this loss function, we find that the weights of the two terms are proportional to the ratio between the size of x and the size of $x ^ { \mathrm { A } }$ , which suggests that we can trade of predictive performance for adversarial robustness by adjusting the relative size of the adversarial sample set. Furthermore, adversarial retraining becomes more efective in enhancing adversarial robustness when coupled with iteration [36]. Multiple iterations of retraining in which new adversarial samples are generated and incorporated into the training set could efectively minimize the upper bound on optimal adversarial risk.

## System Design: The ARText System

Motivated by the extensive application of text classification in predictive analytics, we develop a generalized text classification system with adversarial robustness as an instantiation of our design framework (Figure 2). Specifically, organizations use a wide range of predictive analytics applications based on text classification, such as spam review detection [33], spam email filtering [17], sentiment analysis [61], and adverse event detection [2]. Developing a system capable of assessing and enhancing text classification could significantly benefit these textual predictive analytics applications. Our proposed ARText system generates adversarial samples using a state-of-the-art textual adversarial sample generator, quantifies adversarial robustness with novel measures, classifies texts using bootstrap aggregation of an ensemble of SML models, and further improves adversarial robustness through iterative adversarial retraining.

## Adversarial Robustness Assessment using Adversarial Textual Samples

## Adversarial Sample Generation

ARText’s adversarial sample generation simulates our black-box exploratory attack problem setting. Specifically, we first train a set of substitute models to approximate the target SML model and then leverage the benchmark textual adversarial sample generation algorithm to attack. Following the practice of the state-of-the-art attacks, our substitute model comprises of several traditional text classifiers, such as Naïve Bayes, Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, deep neural network-based text classifiers (e.g., Convolutional Neural Networks), and recurrent neural network-based text classifiers (e.g., Gated Recurrent Networks, and Long Short-Term Memory networks), as well as a homogeneous ensemble learning model, Random Forest. We include most text classification models into our substitute model because adversaries can select various types of substitute models for generating adversarial samples. More importantly, perturbation being added to adversarial samples are model-specific and therefore we can expand the variety of adversarial samples to comprehensively quantify the adversarial robustness. We use the state-of-the-art benchmark textual adversarial sample generator, DeepWordBug, to craft adversarial textual samples [21]. Specifically, DeepWordBug first examines each word in the original text in terms of its impact on the prediction of substitute models and then alters the word with the largest impact by inserting human-readable typos. The adversarial sample generator has state-of-the-art performance in generating adversarial textual samples while maintaining their original semantics, which is a key objective of textual adversarial attacks.

## Adversarial Robustness Measurement

Drawing upon existing performance-based and perturbation-based adversarial robustness measures, ARText proposes novel adversarial robustness measures designed specifically for text classification tasks. In particular, two sets of adversarial robustness measures are proposed in ARText: performance ratio and area under the performance-perturbation curve.

The performance ratio measure primarily seeks to gauge the adversarial attacks’ impact on the SML model’s predictive performance within a given perturbation range. In particular, this measure compares the model’s predictive performance on a non-adversarial dataset against its predictive performance on a mixed dataset comprising both adversarial and non-adversarial samples. Specifically, the mixed dataset is derived from the nonadversarial dataset by perturbing a portion of the non-adversarial samples into adversarial samples with the perturbation range pre-specified by the maximum allowable perturbation $\varepsilon ,$ such that the change in predictive performance could be directly attributed to the adversarial perturbation. The proposed performance ratio measure advances the existing performance-based adversarial robustness measures by teasing out the predictive performance from the adversarial robustness through using the relative predictive performance that incorporates the baseline predictive performance on non-adversarial samples.

Predictive performance for text classification is commonly evaluated using five metrics: accuracy (A), precision (P), recall (R), F-measure (F1), and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC). While existing performance-based robustness measures primarily leverage accuracy, we generalize and extend the idea of performance ratio to the holistic set of text classification metrics. Given the perturbation range ε, we quantify the performance ratio with the following formulation,

$$
R _ {A} (\varepsilon) = \frac {A _ {\mathrm{a}}}{A _ {\mathrm{n}}}, R _ {P} (\varepsilon) = \frac {P _ {\mathrm{a}}}{P _ {\mathrm{n}}}, R _ {R} (\varepsilon) = \frac {R _ {\mathrm{a}}}{R _ {\mathrm{n}}}, R _ {F} (\varepsilon) = \frac {F 1 _ {\mathrm{a}}}{F 1 _ {\mathrm{n}}}, \text { and } R _ {R O C} (\varepsilon) = \frac {R O C _ {\mathrm{a}}}{R O C _ {\mathrm{n}}},
$$

where $\mathrm { m e t r i c } _ { a } \ ( \mathrm { m e t r i c } \in \{ A , P , R , F 1 , R O C \} )$ is measured under the mixed dataset, ${ \mathrm { m e t r i c } } _ { n }$ is measured under the non-adversarial dataset, and $R _ { \mathrm { m e t r i c } } ( \varepsilon )$ is the ratio of classification metric under adversarial attacks within perturbation range ε relative to the non-adversarial context. These measures are non-negative scalar metrics, with a low performance ratio indicating weak adversarial robustness and a high performance ratio suggesting strong adversarial robustness.

Complementing the performance ratio measure is the area under the performanceperturbation curve measure that seeks to capture the trade-of between the perturbation range of adversarial attacks and their impact on predictive performance. In general, perturbation range positively correlates with adversarial attack success, and hence negatively correlates with the predictive performance of the SML model. This is because a wide perturbation range provides the adversarial sample generator with more flexibility to come up with stronger adversarial samples, leading to the diminished predictive performance of the target SML model.

Our proposed performance-perturbation curve aims to characterize the varying predictive performance at diferent levels of the perturbation range. Specifically, the performanceperturbation space is two-dimensional with predictive performance as the Y axis and the perturbation range as the X axis. In the context of text classification, the Y axis is the text classification metric (i.e., accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure, and ROC) and the X axis is the perturbation range, quantified as the percentage of words allowed for perturbation in a sentence, ranging between 0 (no perturbation allowed) to 1.0 (entirely new text). A higher performance-perturbation curve suggests the model is more robust to adversarial attacks across various levels of perturbation range.

The area under the performance-perturbation curve provides an aggregate measure of the adversarial robustness across all levels of the perturbation range. As all text classification metrics are scalar values between 0 and 1.0, the area under the performance-perturbation curve is a scalar metric ranging between 0 (extremely vulnerable) and 1.0 (perfect adversarial robustness). Our proposed area under the performance-perturbation curve measures includes the area under the accuracy-perturbation curve (A/P AUC), the area under the precision-perturbation curve (P/P AUC), the area under the recall-perturbation curve (R/P AUC), the area under the F-measure-perturbation curve (F/P AUC), and the area under the ROC-perturbation curve (ROC/P AUC).

## Adversarial Robustness Enhancement using Ensemble Adversarial Training

## Ensemble Learning

We propose an ensemble learning approach for text classification. Specifically, our proposed ensemble learning approach utilizes bootstrap aggregation (bagging) to improve overall adversarial robustness, where a number of SML models are trained separately, and jointly make decisions through voting. Bagging involves three major steps: first, the training set is bootstrapped into a number of subsamples, each of which is a training set for a constituent SML model; next, each constituent SML model is trained on its bootstrap training set; lastly, given a data point, the predictions are combined using a voting scheme across constituent SML models. As validated in Random Forest, bagging helps to avoid overfitting by reducing variance. Therefore, bagging can efectively decrease the model vulnerability caused by overfitting. Bagging further improves adversarial robustness by increasing the dificulty of conducting

<div class="mineru-algorithm" style="white-space: pre-wrap; font-family:monospace;">
Input: training data  $(x,y)$ ,  $x = [x^{pos}, x^{neg}]$ ,  $y = [y^{pos}, y^{neg}]$ , iteration epoch K, small constant value  $\epsilon$ , number of adversarial samples for retraining I

Output: Adversarial robust bagging SML model f

1: Initialization:  $f^{1} \leftarrow \text{Train}(x, y)$ ,  $k = 1, v^{1} = 0$ 

2: repeat

3: Generate adversarial training data:  $(x_{k}^{\text{A,pos}}, y_{k}^{\text{A,pos}}) \leftarrow \text{AEG\_1}(f^{k}, x^{\text{pos}}, I)$ 

4: Compute classification loss for original data:  $l_{0}^{k} \leftarrow \frac{1}{|x|} \sum_{x_{i} \in x, y_{i} \in y} \mathcal{L}(f^{k}(x_{i}), y_{i})$ 

5: Compute classification loss for adversarial data:  $l_{a}^{k} = \frac{1}{|x_{k}^{\text{A,pos}}|} \sum_{x_{k,i}^{\text{A,pos}} \in x_{k}^{\text{A,pos}}, y_{i}^{\text{A,pos}} \in y_{k}^{\text{A,pos}}} \mathcal{L}(f^{k}(x_{k,i}^{\text{A,pos}}), y_{i}^{\text{A,pos}})$ 

6: Update model:  $f^{k+1} \leftarrow \text{Update}(f^{k}, l_{0}^{k} + l_{a}^{k})$ 

7: Generate adversarial testing data:  $(\widetilde{x}_{k+1}^{\text{A,pos}}, \widetilde{y}_{k+1}^{\text{A,pos}}) \leftarrow \text{AEG\_2}(f^{k+1}, x^{\text{pos}})$ 

8: Compute robustness:  $v^{k+1} \leftarrow \text{AR}(f^{k+1}, \widetilde{x}_{k+1}^{\text{A,pos}}, \widetilde{y}_{k+1}^{\text{A,pos}})$ 

9:Compute the changes:  $\Delta v = v^{k+1} - v^{k}$ 

10:  $k \leftarrow k + 1$ 

11: until k = K or  $\Delta v &lt; \epsilon$ 

12: Obtain final model:  $f \leftarrow f^{k}$
</div>
