Train $( x , y )$ means training given input x and label $y ;$ $\mathsf { U p d a t e } ( f , I )$ means updating f given loss $I ; \mathsf { A E G } _ { - } 1 ( f , x , I )$ means generating I adversarial examples that successfully mislead model f according to samples x (if the number of successful examples is less than I, return those successful examples); $\mathtt { A E G } \_ 2 ( f , x )$ is similar to AEG 1 except it generates adversarial samples for each sample in x but these examples may not mislead model $f . \mathsf { A R } \left( f , x ^ { \mathsf { A } } , y ^ { \mathsf { A } } \right)$ means evaluate the adversarial robustness of model f using the proposed adversarial robustness measures (e.g., performance-perturbation curve based measures) given adversarial example $x ^ { \tt A }$ and corresponding label $y ^ { \tt A } .$

adversarial attacks. For an adversarial sample to be successful in the attack, this sample has to simultaneously exploit vulnerabilities of the majority of the constituent SML models.

Our proposed bagging approach comprises commonly used constituent SML models for text classification.<sup>2</sup> We have both traditional SML models such as Naïve Bayes, Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, and Random Forest, and deep SML models such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) networks [16], and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks [28]. Moreover, we also include bi-directional GRU networks and bi-directional LSTM networks into our constituent SML models due to their widely recognized performance in text classification tasks. In alignment with literature, traditional SML models use the unigram language model to generate bag-of-words features, whereas deep SML models use the original text as the input.

## Adversarial Retraining

The ability of adversarial retraining to incorporate adversarial risk into the objective function of SML model optimization is a distinct advantage. The robustness of our proposed bagging SML model for text classification is further enhanced with adversarial retraining. We propose an iterative adversarial retraining algorithm to optimize our proposed bagging SML model with adversarial samples. The bagging SML model is first initiated with the original training set. In each iteration, we leverage our textual adversarial example generation algorithm to attack the bagging model. Adversarial samples capable of successfully misleading the bagging model are then added to the training set. The augmented training set is used for retraining the bagging model, which is then evaluated in terms of its text classification performance as well as adversarial robustness. Figure 3 presents the detailed algorithm for adversarial retraining.

## Technical Novelties

To summarize, the technical novelties of our ARText system are three-fold. First, we propose two novel measures for adversarial robustness assessment. Compared with the extant performance-based robustness measures, the proposed performance ratio measure advances robustness measurement by teasing out the efect of predictive performance and concentrates on measuring adversarial robustness. Compared with the existing perturbation-based robustness measures, our performance-perturbation curve measure can comprehensively capture the trade-of between the perturbation range of adversarial attacks and their impact on predictive performance. Second, our system innovatively incorporates bootstrap aggregation into iterative adversarial retraining to further advance adversarial robustness enhancement. While prior research uses ensemble learning for generating adversarial samples [52], the ARText system innovatively leverages the diversification strategy for mitigating the risk of adversarial attack by adding bootstrap aggregation to adversarial retraining for robustness enhancement. Lastly, the ARText system constitutes a novel instantiation of our proposed framework. To the best of our knowledge, the ARText system is among the first systems for assessing and enhancing the adversarial robustness of predictive analytics applications on textual data.

## Experimental Evaluation

Consistent with Hevner et al. [27], we rigorously evaluated the efectiveness of the major components of our proposed ARText system through experimental evaluation. In particular, Evaluation 1 examined the utility of the adversarial robustness assessment component. Evaluation 2 evaluated the efectiveness of the adversarial robustness enhancement component. Considering the prevalent application of SML models in the spam detection domain, we evaluated our ARText system on the testbeds of spam reviews and spam emails. In our experiments, we evaluated the ARText system and the baseline SML models in the task of classifying whether a candidate review or email is spam or not. Our spam review testbed is built on a balanced benchmark spam review dataset encompassing 800 genuine reviews and 800 spam reviews for hotels in Chicago [45]. The genuine reviews are collected from well-known online review platforms, including TripAdvisor, Priceline, and Expedia, whereas the spam reviews are labeled on Amazon Mechanical Turk. The spam email testbed is an imbalanced benchmark dataset comprising 2,500 non-spam emails and 500 spam emails. The testbed was collected from Apache SpamAssassin’s public corpus.<sup>3</sup> Our baseline text classifiers included traditional SML models, such as Naïve Bayes (NB), Random Forest (RF), and Support Vector Machine (SVM), deep neural network, such as Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and recurrent neural networks, such as Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) network, Bi-directional GRU (BiGRU), Logistic Regression (LR), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, and Bi-directional LSTM (BiLSTM). Given the model characteristics, the traditional text classifiers used the bag-of-words representation as their input features and the deep neural network and recurrent neural networks used the word sequence as their input features. In our evaluation, we adopted the widely-used 5-fold cross-validation, where the testbed is randomly partitioned into five evenly-sized subsets and the models are iteratively trained on four subsets and tested on a diferent holdout subset. <sup>4</sup> The models’ overall performance is measured by the average of evaluation results across the five holdout subsets.

## Evaluation 1: Adversarial Robustness Assessment

In the first set of evaluations, we sought to demonstrate the utility of the adversarial robustness assessment component. Specifically, we leveraged our proposed performance ratio (in Experiment 1) and performance-perturbation curve (in Experiment 2) robustness measures to gauge the adversarial robustness of the baseline SML models under intra-model transferability-based adversarial attacks. For both testbeds, all models were evaluated on two types of testing datasets, the nonadversarial testing set with original non-spam and spam, and the adversarial testing set mixed with adversarial samples, to calculate our proposed adversarial robustness measures. For each baseline model, the non-adversarial testing set was the same, whereas the adversarial testing set was constructed by replacing the original spam with the adversarial spam reviews using our benchmark textual adversarial sample generator, DeepWordBug, which generated adversarial samples specifically targeting each baseline model.

## Experiment 1: Performance Ratio Robustness Measure

For the performance ratio robustness measure, we mainly compared the predictive performance of the baseline SML models on the non-adversarial testing dataset against their predictive performance on the testing dataset mixed with adversarial samples. The adversarial spam reviews were generated with the perturbation range of 10 percent, where no more than 10 percent of words in the original spam reviews were altered, which was consistent with the practice in prior literature [21].

Figure 4 compares the baseline SML models between the original testing datasets and the testing datasets mixed with adversarial samples on major predictive performance metrics (i.e., accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure, and ROC). On a high level, the performance for all baseline SML models on all metrics decreased on the testing datasets mixed with adversarial spam reviews, underscoring the fact that none of the baseline SML models was inherently robust to adversarial attacks. Moreover, certain models were noticeably less robust than others, in spite of having the best performance on the original non-adversarial testing datasets. For example, LR visually had better performance on all evaluation metrics on the spam review testbed, but this baseline model also had one of the most performance decreases on the mixed spam review dataset. The decrease in predictive performance resulted from adversarial attacks is further quantified by the performance ratio robustness measure.

Table 3 presents the adversarial robustness of the baseline SML models as measured by accuracy robustness $\left( R _ { A } \right)$ , precision robustness $( R _ { P } )$ , recall robustness $\left( R _ { R } \right)$ , F-measure robustness $( R _ { F } )$ , and ROC robustness $( R _ { R O C } )$ . On the balanced spam review testbed, NB achieved the highest accuracy robustness, precision, recall robustness, F-measure robustness, and ROC robustness. While RF attained the second-highest recall robustness, CNN had the second-highest accuracy robustness, precision robustness, F-measure robustness, and ROC robustness. On the imbalanced spam email testbed, RF continued to outperform on recall robustness and F-measure robustness, CNN achieved the best accuracy robustness and ROC robustness, and BiLSTM attained the highest precision robustness. Overall, adversarial samples with the perturbation range of 10 percent were able to compromise standard SML models’ best predictive performance (e.g., precision and recall) by at least 4 to 29 percent on the task of spam detection.

## Experiment 2: Performance-Perturbation Curve Robustness Measures

Performance ratio robustness measure is useful in contexts where the perturbation range is constrained by tools such as grammar and misspelling checks. On platforms where perturbation range is dificult to control, the performance-perturbation curve robustness measure can comprehensively summarize the SML model’s robustness across perturbation ranges by capturing the trade-of between the SML model’s predictive performance on the dataset containing adversarial samples and the range of the perturbation constraints for generating these adversarial samples. Specifically, we evaluated the predictive performance of the baseline SML models at diferent levels of perturbation range, spanning from 0 (no perturbation was applied) to 1 (all words were replaced), and calculated the area under the curve for each baseline model using these data points in the performance-perturbation space. To that end, we created a series of additional testing datasets for each baseline model, each of which replaced the spam reviews in the original testing dataset with adversarial spam reviews generated with a given perturbation range. And we evaluated the predictive performance of baseline SML models on the accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure, and ROC.

Figure 5 gives an example of the recall-perturbation curves of RF and CNN on the spam review testbed. Both curves indicate the negative relationship between recall and the perturbation range: as the perturbation constraint was relaxed, the target SML model became less accurate in detecting spam reviews. However, while RF slightly outperformed CNN on recall at the perturbation level of 0.1 (i.e., the perturbation range of 10 percent), CNN was more robust against adversarial samples on recall in the perturbation range from 10 to 86 percent. The recall of RF converged below 0.3 on the testing dataset containing adversarial samples that had more than 40 percent of words replaced, whereas the accuracy of CNN was almost 0.4 when 40 percent of the words were replaced in adversarial samples and did not converge to 0.3 until 60 percent of the words in the spam review samples were altered. As indicated by the area under the recall-perturbation curve, CNN had higher adversarial robustness over RF.

Table 4 shows the baseline models’ adversarial robustness in the area under the performance-perturbation curves. On the balanced spam review testbed, CNN consistently achieved the best adversarial robustness on all performance-perturbation curve robustness metrics. While NB achieved the best robustness on most performance ratio metrics at the perturbation range of 10 percent, this model failed to outperform other baseline models when evaluated across various levels of perturbation range. BiLSTM attained the best P/P AUC. On both testbeds, R/P AUC was noticeably lower than P/P AUC across baseline models, which explained the low F/P AUC scores. This finding suggests that adversarial attacks induced the baseline models to make significantly more Type II errors. One possible explanation for the adversarial robustness of CNN relative to other baseline methods is that our trained CNN achieved relatively strong Lipschitz properties, indicating relatively high network continuity [4, 49]. According to Szegedy et al. [49], CNN with high continuity had fewer regions of continuities where adversarial examples might reside.

## Evaluation 2: Adversarial Robustness Enhancement

In the second set of evaluations, we conducted a series of experiments to assess the efectiveness of the adversarial robustness enhancement component. Specifically, we gauged the eficacy of the proposed ensemble learning meta-design (Experiment 3) and evaluated the efectiveness of the adversarial retraining algorithm (Experiment 4). In these experiments, we compared our proposed approach with the same set of baseline SML models under the same intra-model transferability-based attack experimental setting. Moreover, we conducted additional sensitivity analysis and gauged the robustness of our proposed system under transferability-based and query-based adversarial attacks (as shown in the Online Supplemental Appendices).

## Experiment 3: Enhancing Adversarial Robustness with Ensemble Learning

In this experiment, we assessed the efectiveness of the proposed ensemble learning component, where the adversarial robustness of our proposed model was compared against that of the baseline SML models. In particular, the adversarial spam samples in the testing set for our ensemble learning method were generated by DeepWordBug using the substitute model that had the same composition as our ensemble learning model. We utilized both performance ratio and performance-perturbation curve robustness measures to assess the adversarial robustness.

The results in Table 5 suggest that, on both testbeds, our proposed ensemble learning model consistently outperformed the baseline SML models on all performance ratio robustness metrics at the perturbation range of 10 percent. On the balanced spam review testbed, ensemble learning improved the accuracy robustness by 0.071, F-measure robustness by 0.104, and ROC robustness by 0.086 on the testing set comprising adversarial spam review samples with 10 percent perturbation range. On the imbalanced spam email testbed, ensemble learning enhanced the accuracy robustness by 0.007, F-measure robustness by 0.007, and ROC robustness by 0.014.

Moreover, Table 6 shows the results of performance-perturbation curve robustness, in which our ensemble learning-based system outperformed all baseline SML models on both testbeds as well. Specifically, the ensemble learning model significantly enhanced A/P AUC by 0.159, P/P AUC by 0.02, R/P AUC by 0.359, F/P AUC by 0.25, and ROC/P AUC by 0.052 on the balanced spam review testbed and advanced A/P AUC by 0.018, P/P AUC by 0.008, R/P AUC by 0.039, F/P AUC by 0.035, and ROC/P AUC by 0.035 on the imbalanced spam email testbed. In sum, our ensemble learning model was more robust to adversarial spam reviews overall. These findings confirm that our ensemble learning model was able to leverage the diversification strategy to mitigate model vulnerability and increase the dificulty of generating successful adversarial spam samples, which needed to exploit vulnerabilities of the majority of the constituent SML models.

## Experiment 4: Enhancing Adversarial Robustness with Adversarial Retraining

This experiment assessed the robustness improvement of SML models attributed to incorporating the proposed adversarial retraining algorithm. Building upon the results from the previous experiment, we introduced the proposed iterative adversarial retraining algorithm to both the ensemble learning model and the baseline models. In particular, the algorithm iteratively combined DeepWordBug-generated adversarial spams with the original spams into a new training set such that, in each iteration, the SML model was trained on this new training set mixed with original and adversarial spams. The number of iterations was bounded at 100 or early convergence as measured by the proposed adversarial robustness metrics. We compared the adversarial robustness before and after the adversarial retraining to gauge the improvement on both performance ratio and performance-perturbation curve robustness measures.

Figure 6 compares the performance ratio robustness before and after adversarial retraining and Table 7 demonstrates the performance ratio robustness improvement results. At the perturbation range of 10 percent, all models improved adversarial robustness on both testbeds after adversarial retraining as measured by performance ratio robustness. As shown in Figure 6, our proposed ARText system achieved the highest adversarial robustness across all performance ratio robustness metrics on both testbeds after adversarial retraining. On the spam review testbed, the recall robustness of our method improved by 29.11 percent, and other metrics improved by at least 2 percent. On the spam email testbed, the recall robustness of our method increased by 26.27 percent. Among the baseline models, both traditional and deep learning SML models had noticeable improvements across all performance ratio robustness metrics on both testbeds.

Figure 7 and Table 8 show the improvement results on the performanceperturbation curve robustness metrics. Across various perturbation levels, both the proposed ARText system and baseline models improved on most performanceperturbation curve robustness metrics after adversarial retraining. Specifically, all models had enhanced performance on accuracy-perturbation curve robustness, recallperturbation curve robustness, F-measure-perturbation curve robustness, and ROCperturbation curve robustness. Overall, adversarial retraining helped the ARText system attain the best performance across all performance-perturbation curve robustness metrics on both testbeds. In particular, the R/P AUC robustness of our method increased by 27 percent on the spam review testbed and by 82 percent on the spam email testbed when adversarial retraining was paired with ensemble learning. While the precision-perturbation curve robustness of CNN and LR failed to improve on the spam review testbed, their performance-perturbation curve robustness of recall had significant improvement after adversarial retraining. This finding suggests that adversarial retraining led to reduced Type II errors and an increased number of adversarial spam samples detected, which has significant implications in our problem setting. Overall, our results indicate that the adversarial retraining algorithm not only improved the adversarial robustness of our ensemble learning model but could also systematically enhance the adversarial robustness of baseline SML models in general. Moreover, ARText outperformed baseline models enhanced by adversarial retraining, confirming that ensemble learning was efective in further advancing adversarial retraining in robustness enhancement.

## Discussion

The experiment results demonstrate the efectiveness of ARText and its underlying metadesign. The first set of evaluations demonstrated the utility of the proposed performance ratio robustness measure and performance-perturbation curve robustness measure. We found that none of the baseline SML models were absolutely robust to adversarial attacks, confirming our research motivation. The second set of evaluations gauged the efectiveness of the two design principles of our ARText system and its underlying meta-design. Our experiment results suggest that both ensemble learning and adversarial retraining were able to significantly enhance the adversarial robustness of our ARText system. Our findings have important design implications for the growing body of IS literature on predictive analytics. The results also provide insights for the broader communities of practitioners developing predictive analytics applications. The major takeaways are three-fold.

First, adversarial robustness should be an integral part of evaluating predictive analytics. Predictive analytics applications are facing greater risks of exploitation as these applications are increasingly utilized for mission-critical decision-making. Our results in Experiment 1 have shown that adversarial samples with the perturbation range of 10 percent could distort standard SML models’ predictive performance such as precision and recall by at least 3 percent and 28 percent on our testbeds. This finding is generalizable to numerous application domains because standard SML models are generally plagued by their vulnerable assumption underlying the widely used empirical risk minimization principle. To account for threats exploiting vulnerabilities of SML models, the predictive analytics literature needs to be extended by incorporating the consideration of potential adversarial threats and the evaluation of adversarial robustness. For organizations, testing the predictive analytics for adversarial robustness is essential for ensuring the security of decisionmaking informed by predictive analytics. Specifically, model selection and optimization should be guided by predictive performance augmented with adversarial robustness in developing predictive analytics applications.

Second, both predictive performance and perturbation provide valuable perspectives for assessing adversarial robustness. As the predictive performance of SML models and the perturbation range of adversarial samples are negatively related, our two proposed robustness measures jointly leverage both for assessing adversarial robustness. The performance ratio robustness measure directly reveals the adversarial attacks’ impact on predictive performance at a given level of perturbation range, which is particularly useful in application domains having fixed perturbation ranges. The performance-perturbation curve robustness measure provides a comprehensive quantification of the trade-of between the model’s predictive performance and the adversarial sample’s perturbation range. This measure can be valuable in application domains where the perturbation range is unbounded and the overall adversarial robustness is preferred. In our study, these measures are instantiated in the context of text classification using classification metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure, and area under ROC; however, these measures are generalizable to other predictive analytics tasks by incorporating predictive performance metrics from the specific application domain.

Third, ensemble learning and adversarial retraining are efective design principles in enhancing adversarial robustness. Ensemble learning enhances adversarial robustness because the diversification strategy is efective in mitigating security risks of adversarial exploitation. Successful adversarial samples have to mislead a majority of the constituent models of the ensemble learning approach. In Experiment 3, ensemble learning improved the accuracy robustness by over 7 percent and F-measure robustness by at least 10 percent on adversarial spam review samples with the 10 percent perturbation range. Adversarial retraining essentially reduces the vulnerable assumption underlying the empirical risk minimization principle by augmenting the training set to account for the distribution of adversarial samples. In Experiment 4, we observed increases up to 29 percent on performance ratio robustness and increases up to 27 percent on performance-perturbation curve robustness when adversarial retraining was paired with ensemble learning. Moreover, these design principles not only provide guidelines for developing new predictive analytics applications but can also be applicable to existing predictive analytics applications seeking to improve their adversarial robustness without significant changes to the underlying SML models.

## Conclusions

Our study makes several key contributions to research and practice. First, we contribute to the emerging literature on AI governance by examining the unique security concern of adversarial attacks facing human-AI hybrids. Specifically, we show that, while an AI system can be evaluated as efective in benign settings, the inherent vulnerability of its underlying algorithm may compromise the efectiveness of the AI system in adversarial attacks. Therefore, the security of AI constitutes a major consideration in developing human-AI hybrids for task substitution, augmentation, and assemblage. Second, we extend the predictive analytics literature by incorporating the adversarial robustness assessment into the evaluation. While the focus of predictive analytics research has been on developing novel algorithms to inform decision-making, we show that predictive analytics-informed decision-making could be threatened by adversarial attacks. As decision-making is increasingly dependent on predictive analytics, we expand the evaluation of the predictive analytics applications by incorporating adversarial robustness. Third, our study makes a design contribution by proposing a design framework based on the technology threat avoidance theory for assessing and enhancing the adversarial robustness of predictive analytics applications. We demonstrated the feasibility of the design framework through developing the ARText system for text classification tasks, which instantiated the design guidelines in its adversarial robustness measures and techniques for ensemble learning and adversarial retraining. A series of experiments were conducted to illustrate the utility and efectiveness of key components of ARText, demonstrating the eficacy of our design guidelines.

This study has important implications for practitioners. As predictive analytics that supports decision-making constitute an increasingly critical endeavor, the adversarial robustness of predictive analytics applications emerges as a paramount concern. Our research can shed light on the significance of this concern to organizations, and the guidelines presented in this study are to mitigate this concern. While predictive performance remains an essential benchmark for predictive analytics, the adversarial robustness emphasized by our proposed framework provides considerable complementary value to allow better decision-making at the risk of adversarial attacks. Moreover, in addition to traditional IT security strategies such as anti-virus, intrusion detection, and identity and access management [37], there is an increasing need for organizations to impose policies and procedures to secure important information about the underlying predictive model in designing, implementing, and operating predictive analytics applications.

This work has several limitations and future research will improve upon our design framework. First, while our proposed framework is efective in assessing and enhancing the adversarial robustness of predictive analytics, the ensemble learning and adversarial retraining design principles entail computational costs. Future research may explore extensions that could improve the computational eficiency of the framework. Second, our framework primarily focuses on enhancing the underlying SML model of predictive analytics. Feature engineering is also an important aspect of predictive analytics and could be potentially vulnerable to adversarial attacks. The attack and defense of diferent feature engineering techniques in real-world problem settings could be a promising future direction. Third, in alignment with prior literature, our research quantifies textual perturbation as the percentage of words perturbed. Under this assumption, inserting a typo had the same implications as replacing a word with its synonym. There could be contexts where this might not be the case and therefore the extent of perturbing words could be further examined, diferentiated, and quantified.
