In our analysis, we use two multiclass classification models that were used in prior literature to construct interpretations of complex models, including decision trees with an application of SHAP TreeExplainer (Lundberg et al. 2020) and interpretable decision sets (IDS) (Lakkaraju et al. 2016). We provide the specifics of these methods and the corresponding measures in Online Appendix G.

## 6. Results

In this section, we present the results of our analysis. First, we compare the clustering performance of the proposed hyperbolic embedding approach with the traditional Euclidean baseline. Second, we evaluate the quality of recommendations produced by our HyperCARS method and compare it with the baselines. Finally, we evaluate the interpretability of the produced hyperbolic contextual situations and compare them with ones produced by the Euclidean approach.

6.1. Quality of Hierarchical Contextual Situations To evaluate the quality of the obtained clustering tree hierarchies produced with methods described in Section 4.2, we follow the evaluation procedure described in Section 5.3. We examine the relationship between the granularity of contextual situations obtained from the clustering tree hierarchy and the corresponding partitioning quality. Figures 6 and 7 present the results of the AHC approach based on the hyperbolic and Euclidean embeddings in terms of the Dunn Index and Silhouette measures calculated for the considered data sets.

The Dunn Index for the Frappe data set presented in Figure 6(a) (top) shows the advantage of Euclidean embedding for a small number of contextual situations (clusters), for example, nine situations. However, the proposed hyperbolic approach consistently outperforms the Euclidean one in the range between 10 and 45 contextual situations. For the higher granularity levels (over 45), both approaches demonstrate similar performance in terms of Dunn Index. The results of Yelp data reported in Figure 6(b) (top) demonstrate the advantage of hyperbolic embeddings in terms of the Dunn Index in the range from 16 to 50 contextual situations. Both Gowalla data sets (Figure 7) demonstrate the advantage of hyperbolic embeddings in the range from 5 to 50 contextual situations. Silhouette measure on Frappe data (Figure 6(a) (bottom)) shows that the Euclidean embedding achieves better partitioning quality for a small number of contextual situations. However, starting from 12 contextual situations, the proposed hyperbolic method consistently outperforms the Euclidean approach. The analysis of the Silhouette measure on other data (Figures 6(b) and 7, (a) and (b) (bottom)) shows similar results, that is, our hyper bolic approach consistently outperforms the Euclidean baseline starting from 18 contextual situations on Yelp, 12 on Gowalla-NYC, and 5 on Gowalla-SF data. Furthermore, we run the same evaluation procedure for the HDBSCAN clustering and report the results in Online Appendix H. Similar to AHC, we observe that for a number of clusters greater than 10 on Frappe, 16 on Yelp, 11 on Gowalla-NYC, and 5 on Gowalla-SF data sets, the proposed hyperbolic approach achieves higher values of Silhouette measure. Figures H3 and H4 in the Online Appendix show that HDBSCAN was able to produce more hierarchical levels with higher granularity on the hyperbolic embeddings for all data sets.

In summary, both clustering measures used in both the AHC and HDBSCAN clustering approaches on all considered data sets show that the proposed hyperbolic approach outperforms Euclidean baseline and provides more flexibility to select distinct granularity levels for the final hierarchy of contextual situations (Section 4.2). It also allows to select more granular levels with higher partitioning quality. Figures 6 and 7 show that for the same large number of clusters, the hyperbolic approach demonstrates higher partitioning quality, which means that the resulting contextual situations are better separated. This comparison shows that the proposed hyperbolic embedding approach works better than its Euclidean counterpart and that the obtained clustering tree hierarchies can produce a more detailed representation of contextual information that will be subsequently used in a recommendation model.

We designed the experiment according to the proposed framework (Figure 1): The comparison of HyperCARS models with the UCAM baseline demonstrates the advantage of using grouped embeddings, and the comparison with the HCAM-Latent baseline demonstrates the advantage of using hyperbolic space over the Euclidean one for modeling hierarchical contextual information (arrow 5 in Figure 1). Table 3 reports the rating prediction performance for the Frappe data set with respect to RMSE and MAE metrics using 10-fold cross-validation (CV), and the task of top-N recommen dations with respect to the Hit@K and MRR@K measures using 10-fold CV. For the Gowalla data set, we present the top-N recommendation results in Table 4 with respect to the Hit@K and MRR@K measures using the time-based splitting. For Yelp, we present the rating prediction results in Table 5 with respect to RMSE and MAE metrics and top-N recommendation performance with respect to the Hit@K and MRR@K measures using the time-based cross-validation splitting.

First, Tables 3–5 show that the context-aware models outperform context-unaware baselines MF and NCF (described in Section 5.2), which confirms that contex tual information is an important factor for recommender systems (Adomavicius et al. (2021). Second, similar to the research findings reported in Unger and Tuzhilin (2020), we observe that context-aware models supporting hierarchical situations (i.e., the Euclideanbased HCAM models and the proposed hyperbolicbased HyperCARS models) consistently achieve better recommendation performance. This observation demonstrates that grouping hierarchical information, represented as latent contextual embeddings in both the Euclidean and hyperbolic spaces (arrows 3 and 4 in the proposed framework shown in Figure 1), can better capture latent contextual information than the nongrouped vector-based embedding counterparts because it better identifies complex contextual situations in the latent space, which in turn positively affects the recommendation performance.

Furthermore, the results show that both HyperCARS models supporting hyperbolic contextual situations that are grouped in a hierarchical manner, achieve significantly better performance than all baselines, including the aforementioned HCAM, across all the metrics and all the data sets. Specifically, for the Frappe data set, HyperCARS models improve the second-best baseline HCAM-Latent model by more than 12% in terms of RMSE and MAE measures. For the Gowalla NYC and SF data sets, HyperCARS models reach the highestranking performance values in terms of the Hit@5 measure, which is an improvement of more than 17% over the second-best baseline HCAM-Latent. We observe that the improvement in terms of Hit@N measures on the Frappe data set is higher than on the Gowalla data sets, which can be attributed to the higher quality of the contextual data on the Frappe data set that was collected directly through the application with no missing values, as well as to the higher density of that data set. Finally, for the Yelp data set, HyperCARS models outperform the second-best baseline HCAM-Latent by more than 6% in terms of RMSE measure and by more than 13% in terms of Hit@5 measure. These observations demonstrate the advantage of grouping latent contextual information in a hierarchical manner and using hyperbolic space over the Euclidean for modeling hierarchical contextual information in CARS (arrow 5 in Figure 1).

6.2.2. Ablation Study. We run the ablation study to understand how the recommendations produced by the HyperCARS method depend on the specifics of its various components. The details are provided in Online Appen dix I. First, the comparison of the $H y p e r C A R S _ { \mathit { S e l e c t e d - L e v e l s } }$ and $H y p e r C A R S _ { C o m p l e t e - T r e e }$ versions of the method show that both significantly outperform all the considered baseline methods. We also observe that the attention mechanism of $H y p e r C A R S _ { C o m p l e t e - T r e e } ,$ which automatically identifies the most important levels in terms of the recommendation performance metrics, in line with the “level selection” criteria, mostly pays attention to the levels that are distinct in granularity and demonstrate high clustering performance.

Second, the evaluation of $H y p e r C A R S _ { S e l e c t e d - L e v e l s }$ model trained using different sets of granularity levels $h _ { t }$ demonstrates the importance of using hierarchical clustering, as it leads to better recommendation performance vis-a´-vis using nonhierarchical clustering. This analysis also demonstrates that it is not sufficient to rely only on the first few levels from the contextual situation tree hierarchy because adding more granula levels leads to better recommendation performance results.

Third, the level-selection sensitivity analysis shows that HyperCARS is not sensitive to the selection of a different set of levels with a high clustering quality. Finally, the comparison of AHC and HDBSCAN methods for generating hierarchical contextual situations shows that the choice of the exact hierarchical clustering technique does not affect the produced recommendation results.

4. Recommendation Performance Results on the Gowalla Data Sets

The AHC results in terms of DT Accuracy, IDS Accuracy, and IDS AUC on the Frappe data set reported in Table 6 show that both DT and IDS methods can fit clusters produced by the hyperbolic embeddings approach significantly better than its Euclidean counterpart. Furthermore, constructed interpretations on hyperbolic embeddings cover significantly more contextual vectors (higher value of DT Coverage@95 and lower value of IDS FU). Finally, the average complexity of the obtained interpretations is significantly lower for the hyperbolic approach in terms of both SHAP Average weight and IDS ARL measures. All the differences are statistically significant with $p \leq 0 . 0 0 1$ . The obtained results for the HDBSCAN approach show that both interpretation methods can fit the hyperbolic-based clusters significantly better for both hierarchical levels, which means that the constructed interpretations of hyperbolic contextual situations are more accurate.

Table 6 also reports the results for Gowalla and Yelp data sets. Similarly, we observe that the interpretations of the hyperbolic contextual situations are significantly more accurate than those produced for the Euclidean clusters. The differences are statistically significant for most of the considered hierarchical levels, besides the least granular level in the AHC hierarchy on Gowalla data sets. Furthermore, interpretations of hyperbolic clusters cover significantly more contextual vectors than those based on Euclidean embeddings. The differences are significant in most of the hierarchical levels. We provide examples of interpretations constructed on the Gowalla-NYC data set on the third level of granularity for the Euclidean and hyperbolic embeddings in Online Appendix J.

In summary, we observe that both interpretation methods can better (more accurately and with better coverage) interpret hierarchical contextual situations produced based on the proposed hyperbolic embedding than the situations produced based on the traditional Euclidean approach.

Euclidean space. Our method, called HyperCARS, implements a loose-coupling approach that allows taking advantage of using hyperbolic space for modeling hierarchical structures of contextual information but, at the same time, provides great flexibility to use a broad range of previously developed recommendation algorithms, and not only in the hyperbolic but also in the Euclidean space. We demonstrate that this new hyperbolic-based approach produces superior performance versus the Euclidean case in terms of identifying and clearly specifying groups of hierarchical contextual situations, providing better contextaware recommendations and better interpretability of the resulting contextual situations.

This superior performance can be attributed to better capturing the hierarchical nature of contextual variables in the latent hyperbolic space. Consequently, the advantage of using HyperCARS over Euclidean embeddings appears in cases when an application deals with a large number of contextual situations that have a complex hierarchical organization, which happens in many practical cases. For example, Netflix collects and uses rich contextual information, including time, user location, weather, screen size, and so on (Baltrunas 2019). Each contextual variable introduces a new dimension in the contextual space, and the number of contextual situations grows exponentially with respect to the number of contextual variables. Therefore, with only a few variables, the hierarchical structure of contextual information quickly becomes complex, which provides an impetus to model it in the hyperbolic space. Furthermore, it has been argued in Adomavicius et al. (2021) that many applications dealing with only a few simple contextual variables, in fact, missed additional contextual dimensions, and various novel methods have been developed on how to find and deploy such additional contextual information (Bauman and

Tuzhilin 2022). Therefore, the contextual space is usually quite complex in many important recommendation applications and may benefit from the use of the proposed hyperbolic-based approach.

Besides the CARS literature, our paper contributes to the IS literature by introducing an approach for using hyperbolic embeddings combined with hierarchical clustering for modeling hierarchically struc tured data that can be subsequently used within the traditional models in a loosely coupled fashion. To this extent, we present the Latent Embeddings Representation Framework (Figure 3) that systematically classifies various approaches to model hierarchical data using hyperbolic versus Euclidean space and nongrouped versus grouped methods. In addition to providing a classification of prior work on embeddings, the proposed framework also paves the way to identifying novel research streams exploring the benefits of hyperbolic spaces across IS applications having hierarchical data (not necessarily only recommender systems).

Our experiments were designed to evaluate various latent embedding representation approaches presented in the proposed framework based on the CARS application. First, the comparison of HyperCARS with the ECAM and HCAM-original baselines shows the advantage of using latent embeddings for modeling contextual information. Second, the improvement over the UCAM model demonstrates the advantage of using grouping for modeling context. The performance advantage over HyperCARS with only a single layer from the tree confirms the importance of using hierarchical clustering within HyperCARS. Finally, the comparison with HCAM-Latent demonstrates the advantage of using hyperbolic space for modeling hierarchical contextual information.

The proposed HyperCARS method has the following practical business implications. First, it leads to better recommendations vis-a´-vis the alternative CARSbased approaches. In particular, as shown in the paper, the absolute values of recommendation performance improvement in the Frappe, and Yelp data sets constitute around 12.91%, and 7.34%, respectively, in terms of RMSE, and around 93.41%, 14.99%, and 19.66% in the Frappe, Gowalla, and Yelp data sets in terms of Hit@3, respectively, which are considered to be very strong results in recommender systems (Hastings 2012, Ricci et al. 2022) that can potentially impact business performance metrics (Panniello et al. 2016). As another example of practical implications of more accurate recommendations, Li et al. (2020) demonstrated that a couple of percentage points improvements in accuracy for short video recommendations for more than 500 million customers on the Alibaba-Youku platform leads to significant improvements in business performance metrics. Better interpretability of the HyperCARS method has another practical implication. Managers need to understand what types of recommendations are provided in which contextual situations, which is hard to do in the latent space. Therefore, the interpretability of latent contextual situations is crucial for them.

As reported in Section 5.1, implementation of the hyperbolic embeddings approach comes with increased computational costs for the embedding construction and calculation of the pairwise distances. Online Appendix K examines how HyperCARS scales with the size of the data set. The aforementioned additional calculations should be done only once and do not need to be updated on a regular basis within the loose-coupling paradigm implemented in HyperCARS. Therefore, these several extra hours of calculations is a small “price” to pay to achieve better recommendation performance of the proposed HyperCARS method vis-a´-vis the alternative approaches.

As a future work, we plan to extend the proposed method by studying the hybrid approach that synergistically combines Euclidean and hyperbolic contextual situations. Furthermore, we plan to study other types of explanation methods and labeling the contextual situations for other applications that may require explanation of contextual information. Finally, we plan to study tightly coupled hyperbolic contextual and recommendation methods that use hyperbolic spaces in an end-toend manner for modeling contextual situations and providing superior context-aware recommendations.
